title: AMMA Finally Acted on a Harassment Complaint — but It Took a Police Filing to Get There
excerpt: The Malayalam film industry's most powerful body reinstated a terminated employee and placed its treasurer on leave. Progress, or just optics?
body:
The Association of Malayalam Movie Artists — better known by its acronym AMMA — just did something it has historically been terrible at: responding to a harassment complaint with actual consequences.

Employee Athulya, who filed complaints with the Kochi City Police and the Labour Office alleging mental harassment by AMMA treasurer Unni Sivapal, has been reinstated after the organisation's executive committee placed Sivapal on leave. It's a small victory, but in an industry still reckoning with the Justice K. Hema Committee's devastating findings, every institutional response is a data point.

## What Happened

According to Athulya's complaint, the harassment by Sivapal extended beyond office hours and involved sustained mental cruelty — not a one-off incident but a pattern. She also named Kukku Parameswaran in her allegations, though no action has been taken against Parameswaran so far. After filing the complaint, Athulya was terminated from her position — a move that triggered immediate backlash.

Actor Shweta Menon, speaking on behalf of the executive committee, confirmed that Athulya's termination was reversed and Sivapal would remain on leave pending investigation. In the same meeting, the committee accepted actor Ansiba Hassan's resignation, which was attributed to "personal reasons."

## The Hema Committee Shadow

You cannot discuss accountability in the Malayalam film industry without mentioning the Justice K. Hema Committee report. Originally compiled in 2019 but kept under wraps for years, the report laid bare a system rotten with casting couch culture, pay disparities, and institutional silence around sexual harassment.

When the report finally surfaced publicly, it triggered a wave of resignations, police complaints, and the formation of a Special Investigation Team. The #MeToo reckoning that followed forced AMMA — long criticised as a boys' club that protected its powerful members — into a corner.

The Sivapal case is different in nature (workplace harassment by a functionary, not sexual assault by a star), but it tests whether AMMA has actually internalised any lessons from the Hema Committee fallout — or whether it's still operating on damage control.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For the millions of Malayalis abroad — in the Gulf, the US, the UK, Canada, and Australia — the Malayalam film industry isn't just entertainment. It's a cultural lifeline. The films, the stars, and yes, the industry's institutional politics are followed with the same intensity as back home.

AMMA's response here will be watched closely. The organisation has over 500 members, including Mohanlal, Mammootty, and virtually every working actor in Kerala cinema. When it acts (or doesn't act) on harassment complaints, it sets a tone for the entire industry.

The reinstatement of Athulya is a positive step. The fact that it took a police complaint and a labour filing to get there is not. And the silence on Kukku Parameswaran's alleged involvement raises the obvious question: is accountability still selective?

## What's Next

Sivapal's leave is described as pending investigation, which means the story isn't over. Whether AMMA follows through with a transparent process — or quietly reinstates Sivapal once the news cycle moves on — will determine whether this was a genuine institutional shift or another exercise in optics.

The Hema Committee proved that silence is the industry's default setting. Breaking that default takes more than one executive committee meeting.
